title: Validsa, Inc. v. PDVSA Services, Inc.
lead: A food trader received an internal message directing cancellation of a large beef order while it held substantial advance payments. Its demands for reassurance led to disputed proposals, a lawsuit, and an appeal separating the buyer’s possible repudiation from its purchasing agent’s liability.

actors.name: Validsa, Inc.
actors.role: Florida international food trader selling beef, chicken, and sugar.

actors.name: Bariven
actors.role: Purchaser and subsidiary of Venezuela’s national oil company, PDVSA.

actors.name: PDVSA Services, Inc. (PSI)
actors.role: Bariven subsidiary acting as its disclosed purchasing agent.

actors.name: Kabboul
actors.role: President of Bariven and PSI involved in disputed communications.

actors.name: Herce
actors.role: Defense economist whose proposed damages testimony was partly excluded.

proceedings: The district court granted Validsa summary judgment, dismissed counterclaims, and conducted a damages trial. The Eleventh Circuit reversed PSI’s liability, remanded Bariven’s disputed anticipatory claims and linked counterclaims, and affirmed independent counterclaim dismissals and specified damages rulings.
limits: The unpublished appeal left assurance adequacy for trial and did not find a bribe demand proved. The $40.76 million damages calculation preceded offset of about $44.58 million in advances; remand instructions were conditional, not an unconditional net award. Later trial outcomes are not supplied.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A Venezuelan buyer contracts for food through its purchasing subsidiary
sections.cue: How were the parties and advances identified?
paragraphs: Validsa, Inc., a Florida international food trader, supplied food during Venezuela’s shortage. Bariven, a subsidiary of Venezuela’s national oil company PDVSA, purchased through its own subsidiary, PDVSA Services, Inc. (PSI). Orders identified Bariven as purchaser, care of PSI, and Validsa invoiced that way.

Eight November 2007 purchases totaled roughly $66 million. The litigation involved contracts 326 and 405 for beef and 368 for chicken. March 2008 orders added contract 632 for 100,000 metric tons of sugar at approximately $44.7 million and contract 757 for 24,000 metric tons of beef at approximately $103.9 million.

Bariven advanced thirty percent on the March orders, about $44.58 million in total. Validsa had to secure the advances with performance bonds and contracted with upstream suppliers. The purchases contemplated installments: seventy percent would be paid after each delivery, with its corresponding thirty percent credited from the advance until final performance. Vessels, containers, ports, production, and inspections could change delivery schedules.

sections.title: A disputed demand and an internal cancellation message create insecurity
paragraphs: Validsa asserted that a businessman demanded a $2 million kickback in March, supposedly requested by Bariven and PSI president Kabboul to preserve the contracts. The defendants disputed the allegation, the connection, and its significance; the appellate opinion did not find that Kabboul demanded a bribe.

On April 15, Validsa accidentally received an internal email chain directing cancellation of contract 757 and suspension of payments. The messages had been sent April 8, but no direct cancellation or request to return advances followed during that interval. The defendants said the messages arose after supplier meetings raising concerns about earlier chicken deliveries. Differences in translations from Spanish were immaterial. No March-contract goods had yet been delivered.

sections.title: Demands for assurances produce proposals without agreement
paragraphs: Validsa demanded an immediate written explanation on April 17. At an April 29 meeting, Kabboul proposed using the advances to pay for the first $44 million of March deliveries, then using letters of credit. That differed from applying thirty percent of the advance to each installment, and the parties did not agree. A planned follow-up did not occur for reasons the record did not establish.

On May 9, Validsa’s counsel demanded adequate assurances within five days. The May 16 answer said the internal messages were not meant for Validsa and should not have been considered. Validsa replied May 22 that no sufficiently concrete response had been given and payments were late.

On June 3, PSI sent a proposed agreement labeled a draft without legal or commercial value and requested comments. It proposed a new delivery schedule, forum clause, reciprocal-performance terms, and substitution of PSI as the payment obligor. Validsa did not respond or contact either company again and sued June 12. The November deliveries were complete, no contract-632 sugar had shipped, and one contract-757 beef installment had arrived. Payments for delivered goods were outstanding, while Validsa retained nearly all the advances.

sections.title: Summary judgment resolves liability before a bench damages trial
sections.cue: What did the parties challenge on appeal?
paragraphs: Validsa sought unpaid delivery prices and anticipatory-repudiation damages on the March contracts. Bariven counterclaimed for breach, unjust enrichment, implied good faith and commercial reasonableness, and accounting. Adopting Validsa’s proposed summary-judgment order, the district court imposed liability on all five claims, found insecurity and written demands, deemed the responses insufficient, suggested that proposed changes themselves repudiated the bargain, and dismissed every counterclaim. It held PSI personally liable despite the disclosed agency.

A bench trial calculated unpaid goods, incidental losses, and lost profits at about $40.76 million before offsetting about $44.58 million in advances. The court excluded some expert evidence and the seller’s consequential losses and denied prejudgment interest.

The defendants appealed anticipatory liability, counterclaim dismissals, and expert exclusion; PSI separately disputed personal liability. Validsa cross-appealed consequential damages, offset or recoupment, and interest on earlier purchases. Bariven did not contest liability for delivered November goods or the first beef installment under 757. Judges Barkett and Hull and District Judge Schlesinger, sitting by designation, decided the appeal without a separate writing, reviewing summary judgment anew and expert admissibility for abuse of discretion.

sections.title: The demand was justified, but the response admitted competing interpretations
sections.cue: Why did adequacy require a trial?
paragraphs: Florida Uniform Commercial Code §672.609 allowed a written demand when reasonable grounds for insecurity arose. Merchant standards governed both grounds and adequacy. Pending assurances, commercially reasonable suspension was allowed for performance whose agreed return had not already been received. Failure to assure within a reasonable time, no more than thirty days, constituted repudiation. Ordinarily these were factual issues, though only one rational conclusion could permit a legal ruling.

The appellate court agreed that Validsa had grounds and made a written demand beginning April 17. But reasonable factfinders could view the April meeting, May 16 explanation, June draft, and unrecalled advances as adequate assurance. Substituting PSI might be an effort to escape Bariven’s duties, or might add security through a United States corporation; revised dates could accommodate delay. An unaccepted draft was neither automatically a modification nor necessarily repudiation.

The district court also could not categorically fix repudiation on April 29. The statutory window after April 17 remained open, and the proposals admitted different interpretations. Earlier delivery delays did not bar Validsa’s demand: they related to advance timing, no time-is-of-the-essence term applied, and defendants had not objected or declared breach. But later termination remained different. Adequate assurances would make Validsa’s termination wrongful; inadequate assurances would establish Bariven’s anticipatory breach.

sections.title: Restored counterclaims follow the unresolved breach, while the agent receives judgment
sections.cue: Which claims survived for which defendant?
paragraphs: The court vacated summary judgment against Bariven on Counts IV and V. It reinstated Bariven’s breach counterclaims, Counts I and II, and good-faith and commercial-reasonableness Counts V and VI, without foreclosing other objections to the latter. Unjust-enrichment Counts III and IV remained dismissed because express contracts governed. Accounting Count VII also failed independently: no fiduciary relationship or complex transaction was established, and an adequate legal remedy existed.

Under the Florida law applied, a disclosed principal’s agent did not owe the contract debt absent an express contrary agreement. Bariven was disclosed, and PSI had not assumed its liabilities. Employee beliefs, PSI’s negotiations, a relationship letter, and the unaccepted June proposal did not establish that agreement. Offering future substitution did not create an existing obligation.
The court reversed PSI’s personal liability and directed judgment for PSI on Validsa’s amended complaint. Its liability did not merely return for another trial.

sections.title: The damages evidence rulings remain tied to their factual foundations
sections.cue: Why were expert and extra-quantity claims excluded?
paragraphs: The court upheld exclusion of parts of defense economist Herce’s testimony. His projected supply-cost increases assumed delay beyond October 31, 2008, renegotiation, an agreed higher price, and correspondence with his market indices, without evidence establishing that chain. His commission deduction imported an 8.4-percent rate from earlier dealings without proving an obligation or that rate for contract 757. Unlike an invoked precedent using actual comparable land sales, his calculations rested on hypothetical future transactions. Properly supported testimony could still be offered at the new trial.

Validsa also sought losses on 20,369 additional tons of beef beyond the 24,000-ton purchase pleaded. An attachment mentioning 44,369 tons did not substitute for explaining that larger claim. The court treated those losses as consequential and followed Florida intermediate authority restricting an aggrieved seller to lost profits and incidental damages. Validsa did not persuasively show the Florida Supreme Court would reject that rule. The holding concerned this governing law and pleaded transaction, not every jurisdiction’s seller remedies.

sections.title: The advances support offset and an equitable denial of interest
sections.cue: What did the mixed appellate disposition require?
paragraphs: Florida’s loss theory generally allowed prejudgment interest once liability and monetary loss were fixed, subject to equitable exceptions. Here the advances exceeded the damages calculation, and accepted findings placed the money in Validsa’s hands before the November payments fell due. Interest would create a windfall rather than compensate deprivation, even though the advances related to other contracts. The court affirmed denial of interest and found no offset error on those facts.

On April 21, 2011, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. PSI was entitled to judgment. Unchallenged delivered-goods liability against Bariven retained the interest and offset treatment. The March anticipatory claims and four linked counterclaims returned for trial; three independently defective counterclaims stayed dismissed.

The remand instructions were conditional. Adequate assurances would defeat anticipatory recovery and require consideration of restored counterclaims; inadequate assurances would establish Bariven’s breach and entitle Validsa to the already calculated damages. This was not an unconditional affirmance of a net money award.
